articles.title: The Director of Too Many Cooks Is Back With Buddy, Mixing the Treacly Sweetness of Kids’ TV With Lots of Sticky Blood
articles.summary: Review: Buddy sees Too Many Cooks director Casper Kelly overcome some significant pacing hitches to deliver a singular horror-comedy that delights in subverting the treacly sweetness of kids’ TV with lots of sticky blood and a smart take on some heavier themes.
articles.body:
Buddy will be released in theaters on Friday, August 28.

It’s hard to overstate just how subversive and incredible Too Many Cooks was when it aired with zero warning/zero fanfare in the dead of night on Adult Swim in 2014. In 11 minutes, director Casper Kelly staged what starts as a send-up of ’80s and ’90s multicam sitcom intros, but rapidly devolves into a medium-breaking, surrealist nightmare. Though Kelly carried that bait-and-switch energy into 2021’s feature-length “Adult Swim Yule Log,” it’s Buddy that feels like the true spiritual successor to Too Many Cooks. Initially presenting as an episode of a lost children’s enrichment program in the vein of Barney & Friends, Buddy similarly uses the saccharine trappings of that medium as a delivery system for an edgy, clever descent into madness.

Before the earworm theme song which opens Buddy is even done, the film’s 1990s-appropriate 4:3 aspect ratio, soundstage-style camera coverage, and cheery aesthetic all wonderfully establish the bounds of its kids show form. Buddy the Unicorn (voiced by Keegan-Michael Key) dopily dotes on the kids that spend all their time at the clubhouse and, along with other anthropomorphized objects, teaches them lessons about dancing or how to responsibly use household cleaning products. The episode ends, the credits roll, and life begins anew the next day. It’s a cycle that, as the kids come to realize, obfuscates more malicious intentions on Buddy’s part. The film’s first act is squarely-focused on reinforcing the slipping of the rose-tinted glasses with which the kids see the world, and Keegan-Michael Key’s vocal performance of the orange unicorn reinforces those tonal shifts well. Key is adept at modulating the lovey-dovey musicality of Buddy’s voice with hints of danger that don’t make things too sinister too quickly, so that when there are bursts of violence early on, they do feel surprising and gnarly.

Buddy wastes no time revealing its central conceit and how it plans to push that forward. One of the kids tires of Buddy pretty much immediately, and the fallout of that slight attracts the curiosity of Freddy (Delaney Quinn), another kid in Buddy’s thrall. Quinn’s performance, like Key’s, is impressive in its control, never getting ahead of where Kelly has pitched the tone at any given point. The rest of the kids who make up Buddy’s gang get the occasional chance to shine, but Freddy’s the only one who really has space to develop her character past a caricature of “kid with fewer lines than the others in an episode of Barney.”

Tone really is the highlight of Buddy: the undercurrent of wickedness which roils into view more and more as the movie goes is very well-managed, and no doubt Kelly’s signature strength. Too Many Cooks has inspired countless imitations in the 12 years since its release, but Buddy proves that Kelly is at the top of his class when it comes to weaponizing smiley, vapid positivity into a dark funhouse of f***ery. The filmmaker revels in revealing more about talking inanimate objects like Strappy (Patton Oswalt), Mr. Mailbox (Eric Bauza), Charlie the Train (Michael Shannon), and to what degree they’re able to see past Buddy’s smokescreen. Oswalt’s Strappy in particular becomes a very enjoyable partner to Freddy and the other kids, and though he never has much dialogue all at once, he makes every line count. Shannon double-dips as a second anthropomorphic character, paired with the movie’s best cameo appearance, in a send-up of a different style of children’s programming that feels especially insane in a movie that already feels especially insane up to that point.

Both Anna Kathleen’s production design and Devon Hawkes Ludlow’s puppet design are real highlights in Buddy, critically important to the movie’s overall success. The primary colors and chunky, cartoonish build quality of the set perfectly thread the needle of Kelly’s obvious inspirations so that no single ingredient in the cosmic gumbo feels too overpowering, which is enough to leave Buddy feeling well-defined enough to stand on its own. Ludlow’s puppet work is multifunctional here and also well-representative of Buddy’s tone, presenting an extremely appealing veneer that has room on the inside for all sorts of viscera and nastiness that’s always satisfying to see spill out into the open. Music is also a huge part of Buddy’s identity, with Kelly’s Too Many Cooks songwriter Shawn Coleman providing sing-songy ditties that feel true to the movie’s lineage and become more important to the experience than you might expect.

Even though the particulars of how Buddy’s mask starts to slip are fun to track, the film’s early adherence to the visual language of children’s shows does wear thin quickly, and pacing does become Buddy’s only significant downfall throughout. That Buddy feels as long as it does even at just 96 minutes is most attributable to how the nature of the story opens doors for the kids to question just why they spend so much time at Buddy’s clubhouse, which in turn leads to them pushing the boundaries of their own existence. The mechanics of how all that fits together gives the movie a stop-and-start quality that leaves the momentum of the full piece lacking. Despite the clarity and strength of the film’s tone being incredibly steady (even if the pacing isn’t), that does draw an outsized amount of attention to the visual inconsistencies that are present. As we the audience watch Buddy, the “home base” look of that fullscreen 4:3 aspect ratio is meant to connote that we’re experiencing the Buddy TV show as reality. But later in the movie, we have cause to see footage from that TV show displayed on widescreen TVs. In those moments, the Buddy TV show is displayed in the more modern 16:9 aspect ratio. This is a nitpick, sure, but the harder a director pushes a high concept like this, the more cohesive small details need to be so as not to break suspension of disbelief. It’s not a major distraction, but creating a world so worthy of close inspection does create a double-edged sword that Kelly occasionally slices himself on.

Buddy’s twists and turns deserve to be preserved as much as possible, but that sense of exhaustion with Buddy’s initial formal identity takes its most interesting turn when Cristin Milioti and Topher Grace’s far-more grounded characters come into play going into act two. When Buddy starts to reveal the shape of where the story is going, Milioti becomes the movie’s MVP. As she becomes aware of Buddy’s true nature, Milioti’s Grace provides the movie with a lot of depth through her skillful, adaptive performance. Her own command of tone is on its strongest display during a truly uncomfortable encounter between her and Buddy, which sees a dark movie go even darker than you may expect. Movies like Five Nights at Freddy’s, Willy’s Wonderland, and Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey have been pushing the stock of “mascot horror” up for years now, but Buddy stands apart in how it calls attention to the dangers of using toxic positivity to distract from darker corners of the day-to-day experience. At a certain point, you do get a really clear sense of where Buddy is going to wind up, but as with life, the journey is the destination here, and Kelly throws more than enough curveballs along the way to keep the somewhat predictable ending from feeling dissatisfying.

articles.title: Lanterns Episode 3 Teaser Reveals First Look at Hal Jordan Wearing Iconic Green Lantern Domino Mask
articles.summary: HBO has published the first teaser for Lanterns Episode 3, and it comes with a first look at Hal Jordan wearing Green Lantern's iconic domino mask.
articles.body:
HBO has published the first teaser for Lanterns Episode 3, and it comes with a first look at Hal Jordan wearing Green Lantern's iconic domino mask.

The network dropped the latest trailer for its DCU show following the conclusion of Episode 2 last night. If you didn't catch it after the credits rolled, the full 42-second Lanterns teaser can now be found on the HBO Max YouTube channel .

Don't worry; it doesn't give away too much. As has already been teased, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) is being set up to be a special part of the DCU as episodes roll out. That means confronting what seems to be a Guardian (played by Laura Linney) and reckoning with his past. If the Lanterns Episode 3 teaser is anything to go by, the Green Lantern-in-training seems to be the star of next week's episode, but the moment that has everyone talking online actually concerns a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment featuring Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler).

John Stewart was born for this. Watch new episodes of #Lanterns on Sundays at 9pm on HBO Max. pic.twitter.com/9SMnO7rINT — HBO Max (@hbomax) August 24, 2026

John Stewart was born for this. Watch new episodes of #Lanterns on Sundays at 9pm on HBO Max. pic.twitter.com/9SMnO7rINT

Just after the 17-second mark, you can see a few frames from an old TV playing what seems to be footage of the news covering Hal Jordan. He appears to be suited up in the same outfit we've seen Chandler wear in the show itself, but the main difference here is his bright-green domino mask.

So far, Chandler has given DC fans a slightly grumpier version of the Green Lantern they might be used to. While he's generally been hailed as a fitting inclusion for the DCU, connecting his character to the one we've seen featured in comic books and animated projects for decades has been a bit difficult for some. Seeing him suited up in full Green Lantern Corps attire seems to have already helped connect those dots for those fans online.

Warning! Spoilers for Lanterns Season 1 Episodes 1 and 2 follow.

All of that said, this may be a little more than an Easter Egg rather than a sneak peek at what this particular costume will eventually look like in motion. For starters, the end of Episode 1 pretty heavily implied that Hal Jordan's days in the DCU are already numbered . The Episode 3 teaser also suggested that we'll be skipping around the timeline yet again, potentially traveling back to 1996. If we do see Hal Jordan sporting his domino mask, those moments may be limited to a few flashback sequences.

New look at Hal Jordan wearing a domino mask in 'LANTERNS'. pic.twitter.com/d20PWHm6II — DC Film News (@DCFilmNews) August 24, 2026

New look at Hal Jordan wearing a domino mask in 'LANTERNS'. pic.twitter.com/d20PWHm6II

MASKED HAL JORDAN YOOOOO #Lanterns pic.twitter.com/R61q87Psp2 — Axel🦇 (@AxelTalksFilm) August 24, 2026

MASKED HAL JORDAN YOOOOO #Lanterns pic.twitter.com/R61q87Psp2

OMG the concept of having to wait another week pic.twitter.com/yOcGKss712 — stuff (@stuffiseeonline) August 24, 2026

OMG the concept of having to wait another week pic.twitter.com/yOcGKss712

Still, it's easy to see why fans might be excited for such a relatively small development. The last time we saw a live-action Hal Jordan wearing the mask was when Ryan Reynolds played the character for his 2011 standalone movie, and we all know how that went.

As the DCU comes together, moments like these can be just as important as the projects themselves. Fans clamored for a first look at Robert Pattinson as Batman and again flocked to see him throw on the cowl for The Batman Part 2 . David Corenswet's Superman drew eyes when his costume was revealed back in 2024 .

As Hal Jordan seemingly winds down his time as a Green Lantern, we've yet to see what Pierre's John Stewart looks like in the suit. We'll hopefully get a better look when he reprises his role for the DCU's Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow , next year.

While we wait for Lanterns Episode 3 this weekend, August 30, you can see what IGN thought of Episode 2 . You can also learn about the villain some viewers think is hiding in plain sight , as well as what DC Studios co-CEO James Gunn had to say about the gritty tone for the new DCU series .

articles.title: These Huge One-Volume History Books Are on Sale for $0.99 Each
articles.summary: Two major one-volume history books published by Penguin are on sale for $0.99 each. The deal ends soon.
articles.body:
Heads up, amateur historians: here’s an incredible deal on two beefy tomes for your digital bookshelf. Penguin is running $0.99 sales on the Kindle ebook version of two of its biggest history books. The latest editions of The Penguin History of the World ( see at Amazon ) and The Penguin History of the United States of America ( see on Amazon ) are both on sale for $0.99 each . The sale ends tonight, so grab ‘em if you want to learn a thing or two for super cheap.

The Penguin History of the World: 6th Edition (Kindle Ebook)

The Penguin History of the World is currently in its 6th edition. It’s been a landmark book ever since J.M. Roberts published the first edition in 1976. Roberts was a renowned and popular British historian who updated the book many times over the ensuing decades until his death in 2003. At that point, Penguin brought on the wonderfully named historian Odd Arne Westad to continue editing and revising the tome. In physical form, it’s a doorstopper of a book, ringing in at 1,280 pages. If you grab this deal, the math works out to roughly $0.00077 per page.

The Penguin History of the United States of America: New Edition (Kindle Ebook)

As for The Penguin History of the USA, it was first published in 1985 as The Longman History of the United States of America. It’s by Hugh Brogan , a British historian and biographer who, it so happens, used to correspond regularly with J.R.R. Tolkien. In fact, a number of Tokien's letters to Brogan are included in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien ( see at Amazon ). Anyway, this book kicks off in 30,000 BCE, when it’s thought the first humans may have come over the land-bridge that’s now the Bering Strait, and runs up to the Reagan era of the 1980s.

If you’re like me and you’re not exactly a history buff , but you’re generally interested history as a concept, it can be hard to find good books to read. Most history books, after all, hone in on one time period, or one major historical event. That’s how historians (and most academics and professionals, for that matter) work: they specialize. But if you want a broad overview of all of human history? Or of the history of the United States? Decent one-volume books on those broad topics, that cover that much history, are a bit harder to find.

Penguin’s pair of history books are some of the most popular, and have been for decades. They go in chronological order, so you can follow the broad arc of history over centuries or millennia.

Again, the deals won’t last forever. There’s actually a ticking clock on the page for the USA history book; that deal ends at midnight Pacific Time. As for the History of the World, that one doesn’t have so definite an end, but you can bet it won’t be a buck forever, so add it to your Kindle library sooner than later if you’re interested.

articles.title: This Legend of Zelda Brain Teaser Recreates One of the Best Side Quests From Tears of the Kingdom
articles.body:
Tears of the Kingdom was an excellent game. IGN even went as far as to call it a perfect 10 out of 10 when it first came out on the Switch. And while the boss battles, gameplay, and massive open world definitely contributed to its masterpiece status, it was all of the little side quests that brought it all together for me.

One particular quest that made TotK's Ultrahand abilities shine was helping Addison put up President Hudson signs throughout Hyrule. Now, in 2026, that very quest has been brought into the real world with a brain teaser puzzle.

Legend of Zelda Addison Sign Hanayama Metal Brain Teaser

You have a lot less material to work with than many of the sign puzzles in the actual game, so you can't just start sticking massive boards to the bottom of the sign to keep it upright. Instead, you need to find a very specific solution.

Along with the sign (made of metal) and Addison himself, you have four metal logs to work with. The product page calls it "worthy of a level 6" challenge, so I wouldn't expect the solution to be straightforward.

Once you actually complete the brain teaser, you'll have a little metal figure of Addison and his President Hudson sign you can display on your desk or shelf. The Bepuzzled brand has several other Legend of Zelda-themed puzzles you can check out as well, including the Hyrule Crest and a Master Sword.

The Legend of Zelda Legendary Edition Manga Box Set

Hero of Time: Music From Ocarina of Time 2LP Vinyl

Link With Sound Hallmark Keepsake Ornament

If you (or a Zelda fan you know) are in the market for cool Legend of Zelda merch, there's certainly no shortage of things you can buy. In addition to the game itself, there's a number of Legend of Zelda books and manga worthy of being added to your shelf. We've curated some of our favorites gifts for fans of the franchise , but there's a lot more where that came from.

articles.title: France and Saudi Arabia to Build $7 Billion Dragon Ball Z Theme Park Outside Paris
articles.summary: France and Saudi Arabia have come to the mutual conclusion that the world needs Dragon Ball Z theme park. So, they’re building one near Paris to the tune of €6 billion ($7 billion USD).
articles.body:
France and Saudi Arabia have come to the mutual conclusion that the world needs Dragon Ball Z theme park. So, they’re building one near Paris to the tune of €6 billion ($7 billion USD).

The Elysee Palace announced the news on Monday, August 23, during the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Paris. The idea was reportedly first sparked during the Crown Prince’s trip to the city last year, when he and French President Emmanuel Macron discovered their shared love for the iconic anime franchise.

The park will be constructed northwest of the capital city near Cergy-Pontoise, with the massive project expected to create approximately 22,000 jobs. Construction is predicted to take several years, with no opening date publicly announced as yet.

To no one’s surprise, Qiddiya is providing the funds for the project, which will be one of two Dragon Ball Z theme parks once all is said and done. The first theme park was officially revealed on the official Dragon Ball website back in 2024, along with extensive concept art and teasers for what it’ll look like when construction is complete.

The first park is currently being built in Qiddiya City, a massive entertainment hub currently in development just outside the capital of Riyadh. It will reportedly span more than 500,000 square meters, featuring seven recreations of locales from the series including the Kame House, Capsule Corporation, and Beerus's Planet.

Five rides will also be included as part of a 30+ attraction total, along with a 70-meter-tall statue of Shenron. It’s a massive undertaking, and one that isn’t expected to open anytime soon, with no official opening date released at the time of writing.

Dragon Ball Z Theme Park Concept Art (2024)

The announcement of Paris’s Dragon Ball theme park comes after the Esports World Cup was relocated to the city due to security concerns near Riyadh, where it was previously scheduled to take place. Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince was in attendance for the competition’s closing ceremony, where Macron was also present.

This is one of several expansive investments the country has made into cultural projects within the gaming and anime space; most recently, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund completed a $55 billion acquisition of EA as part of an investor group alongside Silver Lake and Affinity Partners.

In March, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman's Electronic Gaming Development Company (EGDC) acquired a 5% stake in Capcom, upping its ownership in the famed Japanese game developer and publisher to 10%.

And back in February, Saudi-owned RTS took full ownership of Evo , the world’s largest fighting game tournament series, which has since expanded to include several other global Evo events in a controversial turn of events within the fighting game community.

articles.title: Canceled Iron Man Game Footage From Just Cause and Mad Max Developer Leaks Online
articles.summary: Alleged footage from Avalanche Studios' canceled Iron Man game has surfaced online.
articles.body:
Alleged footage from Avalanche Studios' canceled Iron Man game has surfaced online.

In the early 2010s, Just Cause and Mad Max developer Avalanche Studios was working on an Iron Man game . The project was never officially announced to the public, but Avalanche Studios co-founder Christofer Sundberg confirmed its development and cancellation during an interview in 2022. Now, gameplay for that title has popped up online via Reddit , reportedly sourced through a PS3 developer kit.

The gameplay is extremely unfinished, but it shows Iron Man flying around in a large environment, fighting jets and attacking various facilities. One of the more in-depth videos appears to be an unfinished E3 demo which shows Iron Man in hand-to-hand combat with soldiers, using a heavy, Arkham-esque style of combat. Of course, he also boasts his repulsors, missiles, and other gadgets to help take down all of his targets.

One of the more standout features is that the environments would've been at least semi-destructible. Iron Man can throw foes through walls, slice them apart in order to make shortcuts for himself, and tear up buildings around him. Beyond that, the build isn't far along enough to really distinguish itself much from SEGA's MCU Iron Man games. It certainly shows promise, though. Given how fun the studio's Mad Max game is and the sandbox gameplay of the Just Cause series, Avalanche probably would've made a killer Iron Man game.

There is still some hope, however. EA Motive is currently developing a new Iron Man game , though details on the project are extremely scarce. The project entered development in 2022, but there haven't been any updates since then. EA was also working on a Black Panther game, which was canceled last year . However, Iron Man has remained in development, despite fears that it will suffer the same fate. Given it has been four years since the announcement, hopefully we are close to hearing some news on the title.

articles.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Devs Vow to Update Captain Price After Botched Haircut Goes Viral
articles.summary: Publisher Activision and developer Infinity Ward have promised to update Captain Price's hair in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 after images of his botched haircut went viral.
articles.body:
Publisher Activision and developer Infinity Ward have promised to update Captain Price's hair in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 after images of his botched haircut went viral.

As last weekend's closed beta dredged up conversations revolving around its time-to-kill (TTK) speeds and problematic spawn placements, other fans aimed at Captain Price and his barber. It's mostly thanks to a few images that have circulated across social media, with fans pointing out that, maybe, Modern Warfare 4's version of the classic character should invest in some hair gel.

He looks…unwell, at least when compared to past versions of Captain Price. Whether he's chasing down Vladimir Makarov or walking you through a training course, Price is known to have a full head of hair and a beard that could make even Ghost blush. The one from Modern Warfare 4, however, has neither of those things, and according to many, he hardly looks like the Task Force 141 leader fans have come to know. Activision and Infinity Ward say that's not their intention, but there's also a good reason why only some Call of Duty fans are encountering this choppy imposter.

bro.... https://t.co/JxOTxMTny3 pic.twitter.com/WQEHOTgdEU

that ain't captain Price that's lieutenant Cost https://t.co/gtAFT18NhF — narancia gaming (@naranciagaming) August 24, 2026

that ain't captain Price that's lieutenant Cost https://t.co/gtAFT18NhF

That ain’t price that’s amount — IPhantom369 (@CJerome369) August 23, 2026

While the Captain Price making the rounds online does appear to be real, he'll only look this way in Modern Warfare 4 if users tune their devices to the lowest possible settings. Some had expected this to be the case, as reports of the botched haircut seemed to mostly be few and far between.

Still, the developers and Activision and Infinity Ward are going to do their best to give the Call of Duty fan-favorite Operator the head of hair he deserves. The studio community teams X/Twitter account replied to a few of the more popular posts, promising it would be addressed "in a future update."

"Captain Price's hair does not appear correctly when viewing his character model at the lowest level of detail," a tab in the "Known Issues" column from the Modern Warfare 4 Trello says.

Hello! We're aware of an issue with Price's hair not appearing correctly when viewed at the lowest level of detail. The team will be addressing it in a future update. Ultimately this will not be an issue if players meet our recommended specs. Details: https://t.co/uozRRLS3W5 — CallofDutyCM (@CallofDutyCM) August 24, 2026

Hello! We're aware of an issue with Price's hair not appearing correctly when viewed at the lowest level of detail. The team will be addressing it in a future update. Ultimately this will not be an issue if players meet our recommended specs. Details: https://t.co/uozRRLS3W5

What in the 1050 TI is this? Whoever took that screenshot got the game at ultra low, ultra performance, 11% resolution. pic.twitter.com/Pq3A5BdzFt — The Natty One (@lunatty787) August 23, 2026

What in the 1050 TI is this? Whoever took that screenshot got the game at ultra low, ultra performance, 11% resolution. pic.twitter.com/Pq3A5BdzFt

What exactly that update entails remains to be seen, but it's far from the only thing on the team's list. Also noted in the Known Issues category are dropped framerates when cooking lethal weapons, hitches for PC players during their first multiplayer matches, a stuck loadout screen bug, and more. TTK is another issue the team is looking into , as are those spawns.

So, if you find yourself dissatisfied with the Modern Warfare 4 beta, you might want to take another crack at it when the open beta launches this weekend . You can learn more about everything it comes with, including its single-player mission, here .

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has a release date of October 23, 2026, for PC, Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X | S. For more, you can read about how it will allow players to remove masks for some of its Operators . You can also check out IGN's interview with the team to learn about Infinity Ward's approach to matchmaking, the beta, and more.

articles.title: Persona Comes to Beard Papa's With Special 30th Anniversary Collaboration
articles.summary: Beard Papa’s is teaming up with Persona to celebrate the RPG series’ 30th anniversary with some special cream puffs.
articles.body:
Beard Papa’s is teaming up with Persona to celebrate the RPG series’ 30th anniversary with some special cream puffs.

Beard Papa’s is a Japanese dessert chain with locations sprinkled across the US. It’s best known for its primary offering, cream puffs, which come in a variety of different flavors and combinations for customers to choose from.

Starting September 4, participating Beard Papa’s locations within the United States will transform their interiors and offer up several new flavors of cream puffs in collaboration with Persona.

Persona 4 Revival Release Date Trailer Xbox Games Showcase 2026 - Screenshots

These storefronts will feature Persona-themed digital menu boards, bakery case graphics, posters, television displays, and more, transforming them into a real-life Persona menu screen. And for mega-fans, the Beard Papa’s locations in Little Tokyo and Cerritos will include large-format anniversary murals specifically designed for photo opportunities.

Limited-time cream puff flavors are also on offer: Original Cream Puff, Matcha Cream Puff, Ube S'mores Cream Puff, Cookies & Cream Cream Puff, and the Double Berry Cream Puff, each inspired by specific games in the Persona series.

Four and six-pack gift sets are also available for purchase. The four-pack set comes with four featured cream puffs, a Persona chibi sticker sheet, and an in-game code card for Persona 5: The Phantom X. The six-pack set comes with six cream puffs, a blind-packed acrylic standee featuring one of eight designs, and an in-game code card for Persona 5: The Phantom X.

Of course, it wouldn’t be a collab if there wasn’t merchandise involved; you can also snag a ceramic mug, a T-shirt, zip hoodie, and eco tote bag as part of the Persona x Beard Papa’s partnership on the official Beard Papa’s website .

This collaboration lasts from September 4 to October 4, just in time to herald the next big developments for the Persona series. Persona 4 Revival, a full remake of Persona 4 Golden, is set to release in February 2027 , and Atlus is hard at work on the next entry in the franchise, Persona 6.

It’s a big time for Persona; a live-action adaptation is in the works at Netflix, with Christopher Monfette attached as writer, showrunner, and executive producer. 21 Laps' Shawn Levy and Robert Atwood are also attached to executive produce, alongside Sega’s Toru Nakahara.

Beyond that, Kazuhisa Wada, producer for Atlus' P-Studio, recently remarked that he believes the studio will “have to” do remakes of the first and second games in the Persona series, giving fans even more to look forward to as the days tick down to Persona 4 Revival’s release.

articles.title: Xbox and PlayStation Appear to Be Publicly Backing Down from Promoting Multiplatform Releases
articles.summary: Xbox and PlayStation seem to be downplaying their multiplatform presence in new marketing beats.
articles.body:
Xbox and PlayStation seem to be downplaying their multiplatform presence in new marketing beats.

As spotted by PushSquare , Xbox uploaded a new trailer for Minecraft Dungeons 2 on its YouTube channel, which doesn't make any mention of the game coming to PS5 or Nintendo Switch 2. However, the game's previous two trailers, released in March and June respectively, both clearly advertised every platform the title will be released on. It seems like Xbox may be pulling back even further on promoting its games for other platforms now under CEO Asha Sharma.

Earlier this summer, Xbox reportedly pulled the plug on a PS5 version of Gears of War: E-Day just ahead of its reveal. A piece of key art for the game was even shown on an Xbox podcast with a PS5 logo , which was later removed, indicating the decision may have been relatively last-minute. There were also reports that Microsoft pulled a trailer for Halo: Campaign Evolved from a PlayStation State of Play, a move by Sharma that reportedly created tensions between Xbox and PlayStation. It seems like Minecraft Dungeon 2's new trailer may be part of Xbox's strategy to bring players back into its own ecosystem and create brand strength.

Xbox isn't the only one changing its messaging, though. Earlier this year, it was reported that PlayStation is abandoning PC releases for its flashy first-party single-player games like Ghost of Yotei. The company had been releasing the majority of its first-party story-driven games on PC for about half a decade, but it doesn't appear to be part of the strategy going forward. As a result, PlayStation has embraced the "only on PlayStation" branding once again.

In a new PlayStation ad, the words "PlayStation 5 exclusive" are plastered across gameplay for Marvel's Wolverine, Ghost of Yotei, Astro Bot, Gran Turismo 7, Saros, and God of War Laufey. This is meant to signal to players that these games won't be making the jump to PC later and that the company is embracing full-blown exclusivity as it did for decades with the PS1, PS2, PS3, and some of the PS4 generation.

Xbox's strategy still seems a bit wishy-washy, on the other hand. The company has promised permanent exclusivity for Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution , but beyond that, it remains to be seen what will happen. Will The Elder Scrolls 6 be exclusive to Xbox? Will the Fallout 3 and New Vegas remasters be exclusive? Only time will tell.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Songs of the Past Expansion Confirmed to Include More Gwent, and Everyone Is Already Celebrating
articles.summary: CD Projekt Red has confirmed The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion will come with more Gwent, and card game lovers are already celebrating.
articles.body:
CD Projekt Red has confirmed The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt 's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion will come with more Gwent, and card game lovers are already celebrating.

The Witcher 3 earned a lot of praise when it launched back in 2015. While Doug Cockle 's gravelly delivery as Geralt helped sell its story, and its RPG gameplay quickly hooked in every kind of fantasy fan, many would say Gwent was what truly kept them coming back for more.

"In Gwent, gamers clash with friends in fast-paced duels that combine skill-based play with bluffing, and careful deck construction," an official description from CD Projekt Red says . "The game is played over a best-of-three series of rounds, as players unleash their hand by slinging spells and diverse units with special abilities, and use clever tricks to deceive their opponents."

CD Projekt Red's in-universe card game first launched within the third installment in its Witcher series before being transformed into a standalone spinoff in 2017 and a real-life tabletop experience in 2025. It's a formula others have unsuccessfully attempted to mimic, but few have managed to stand the test of time quite like Gwent. That's probably exactly why it will be making a comeback when the developer returns to The Witcher 3 with its Songs of the Past expansion in 2027.

CD Projekt Red community and social media manager Marcin Łukaszewski teased the return of the fan-favorite side activity when replying to a player on X/Twitter . When the fan said they hoped more Gwent would be included in the surprise expansion, Łukaszewski offered a simple reply: "Confirmed!"

It's been more than 10 years since The Witcher 3's last expansion, Blood and Wine, came out in 2016, and by the time Songs of the Past launches next year, that wait will have been even longer. CD Projekt Red has teased that this is a full-fledged add-on for the game's story, teasing earlier this year that it will serve as a prologue . In other words, don't expect it to be all Gwent all the time, but for those who have waited to sit down for another round of tabletop challenges, it sounds like there's already more than enough reason to be excited.

articles.title: Lenovo confirms Legion Go issues after gamers report bricked devices
articles.summary: ﻿I installed Lenovo’s forbidden BIOS and my Legion Go lived. You might be less lucky.
articles.body: When a company’s software update turns your computer into a useless brick, should fixes be free? Framework, the modular computer startup, apparently thinks so. But it’s not clear that computing giant Lenovo will go that far. Three weeks after a Redditor presented a nearly $300 repair bill for their handheld gaming PC — among other reports of damage and high repair bills — the company is breaking its silence. It says, in short: try holding down the power button longer, and if that fails, contact customer support. Here’s the statement Lenovo provided to The Verge, via communications director Jeff Witt: > Lenovo is aware that some Legion Go devices may experience a blank screen during installation of BIOS version V42. BIOS V42 was not distributed through Windows Update or Legion Space, and Lenovo has removed the update from its support website while we continue our validation work. Users who have successfully completed the V42 update should not need to take further action at this time. > If a device encounters a blank screen during V42 installation, users may try pressing and holding the power button for approximately 10 seconds, waiting approximately one minute, and then powering the device on again. If the device does not resume normal operation, customers should contact Lenovo Support for further assistance. > Lenovo continues to evaluate and validate future BIOS updates for Legion Go. On the official Lenovo forums, it appears another Lenovo employee may have weighed in, too: a “Daniel_Legion” claims the issue “should be repaired free of charge” if you’re under warranty. “In the case of out-of-warranty devices, it should be repaired free of charge, but please check local laws,” they write. [Image: The Lenovo forum topic where Daniel_Legion weighs in. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/chrome_jRP4X1wMCS.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] But Daniel_Legion has no other visible posts on the Lenovo forums, and “we’ll repair it if local laws force us to” isn’t a particularly reassuring pitch, so we’re asking Lenovo to confirm his words and their meaning. Will Lenovo extend its warranty to cover bad BIOS bricks? It’s important to note that not every Legion Go was vulnerable to begin with. You’d need to have the original Legion Go 8APU1, not the Legion Go S or the Legion Go 2, and you would’ve had to download BIOS V42 (N3CN42WW) directly from the company’s website over the two or so months before Lenovo yanked it. Even then, you might have been safe. The other day, I chose violence and decided to install the forbidden BIOS V42 on my own Legion Go review unit, and… after a long, scary sequence of black screens and progress bars and warnings and more black screens that lasted six whole minutes, it booted up just fine. (Plays games, even lets me log into Windows by typing my PIN with the gamepad controls. I couldn’t do that right before the update.) [Image: BIOS V42 running fine on my Legion Go. Plays games and everything. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-legion-go-sean-hollister-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Assuming Daniel_Legion is legit, it sounds like the investigation is still ongoing. A team in Europe was able to reproduce the issue with three out of three devices tested, but other teams weren’t able to see it at all, he told the Lenovo forums. “As such the issue is most likely related to specific component used on mainboards in certain batch or batches, or the issue needs to have specific circumstances to manifest,” he wrote. I strongly feel that a company shouldn’t need to fully investigate before reassuring customers. They should say “if we did it, we will fix it, even outside of warranty.” That’s what Framework did with its device-bricking BIOS update.

articles.title: Jason David Frank's Final Movie, Legend of the White Dragon, Won’t Be as Memorable as He Was
articles.summary: Legend of the White Dragon review: Jason David Frank's final movie won’t be as memorable as he was.
articles.body:
Legend of the White Dragon will be released in theaters on August 28.

Let’s get one thing straight up front: Legend of the White Dragon is not a Power Rangers movie.

Yes, for those of my generation that grew up watching Power Rangers, it does include plenty of familiar faces, putting the late Jason David Frank (Mighty Morphin Power Rangers) as well as Jason Faunt (Time Force) and Ciara Hanna (Megaforce) front and center in what is a clear nostalgia play to draw in fans of the original shows. There are even moments in the movie where, if you really squint hard enough, it can almost look and feel like a more adult version of a Power Rangers show… not in the way that the largely forgotten 2017 movie did, but in how the visual effects are often quite shaky and there’s a big ol’ heaping of earnest cheesiness poured over it. It all makes this Kickstarter-funded project play more like a YouTube fan film than a standalone work, but there can be a charm to such an endeavor, and there is something admirable in the abstract about a group of people coming together to make a movie like this.

Unfortunately, while there remains plenty of actual charm in the shows this movie’s cast became known for, that’s utterly lacking in the execution here as the entire thing comes apart with shocking speed. Even as it was able to create its own thing, Legend of the White Dragon feels like a sequel weighed down by a whole series of movies that nobody in the audience has actually seen. There are flashbacks on top of flashbacks, pages of stilted dialogue in one belabored exposition scene after another, and woefully stiff fight sequences that never leave much of a mark. While a movie like this doesn’t need to be as thrilling and kinetic as the recent action stunner, The Furious , it’s still tough going when it can’t actually land a believable punch. More closely resembling the works of Neil Breen — the ultra-low-budget filmmaker known for Double Down, Fateful Findings, and Twisted Pair — but with some more money to throw at things, it’s occasionally unintentionally funny, though mostly a drag.

Our hero-turned-pariah is Erik Reed (Frank); he is believed by many to be, if not in hiding, dead following what characters refer to as "Dark Day," which is essentially a battle he took part in that killed 1,263 innocent people. Don’t worry about remembering any of this: Everything, including this exact number, will get repeated over and over as the movie spends far too long arranging and rearranging deck chairs before it feels like it’s actually even properly starting. Though we’re informed Erik was more of a treasure hunter than a superhero — leading to the hilarious line, “he left behind his most precious treasures, his wife and child” — he’ll soon have to step up and become one when he gets hunted down by those looking to take him in or get revenge. It’s all shallow and broad with a simulacrum of a complex and engaging central superhero character. Sure, he has abilities that come from a crystal which make him so powerful that he can fly into the sky, but while the story builds to him being unleashed to do so, the actual movie surrounding him doesn’t come remotely close to taking flight.

It’s at the secluded boxing ring where Erik has been hiding, which comes complete with old newspaper clippings taped on the wall that outline what we’ve already been told has happened, where we get our first fight. What could have been a goofy brawl, with fighters leaping through the air like wrestlers and smashing concrete blocks on heads, doesn’t actually cut loose. For one thing, the smashing of the concrete block comes down on a motorcycle helmet clearly meant to hide a stunt performer, leaving no sense of actual impact. Even more disappointing, the shaky camera work further obscures the stunts rather than letting us see the choreography clearly. Fight sequences not only can but should be a dance, with camera and performer working together; in Legend of the White Dragon, each proves to have two left feet, never once feeling in sync with the other as it all just shuffles along.

The longer this drags on, the more this ostensibly stand-alone movie just feels like it was conceived to bring together the cast without any thought about what that would actually look like. Once the first already clunky action scene comes to a close, there are large stretches where the film just spins its wheels, leaning heavily on the recurring presence of King Bach as a hologram to explain what’s going on. This may sound on paper like it could be a bit silly or even fun, but there’s no playfulness here. No matter how much the cast is all game, the atrocious dialogue and general lack of movement makes it a scattered slog. Even with brief moments where the actors bounce off each other in some more potentially fun ways, it always falls back to flashbacks which bring everything to a screeching halt, or bits with a one-note villain who can’t create a truly menacing presence.

When the final big confrontation and forced tease for a sequel arrives, you’re left wondering how a movie less than 90 minutes long can feel like it’s pushing two hours. Fans of the cast might still just be glad to spend time with their favorite actors, but both they and the performers deserve better than the slapped-together final film we get here. Despite all the legacies it's gesturing toward and the memorable ensemble it showcases, Legend of the White Dragon is nothing more than a forgettable misfire and miles away from legendary.

articles.title: The TCL Note A1 is a kinder, gentler tablet
articles.summary: It’s easy on the eyes, comes with a stylus, and got me to write out an 1,100 word review by hand. But it isn’t E-Ink.
articles.body: Without thinking, I scribbled over what I’d just written.  It’s what I would have done if I was writing with pen and paper. But I didn’t have a pen in my hand; my canvas was an LCD and the letters on my page were just pixels. Score one point to the TCL Note A1. TCL’s Note A1 Nxtpaper tablet (its full government name) is supposed to make you forget that you’re using a tablet. It has one of the company’s signature low-glare matte displays and ships with a stylus. The pen’s haptics even mimic the scratching of a pencil on paper. On the software side, the A1 takes a lot of cues from the Remarkable tablet. Instead of a typical Android home screen, you get a page with shortcuts to recent notes and a snapshot of the day’s calendar events. You can download any app you want from the Google Play Store, but that would spoil what I think is the A1’s nicest feature: the ability to trick you into forgetting that you’re using a gadget at all. [Product: TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H5K8NBZS?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fgo.skimresources.com%3Fid%3D1025X1701640%26xs%3D1%26url%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fus.tcl.com%252Fproducts%252Ftcl-a1-note] The Note A1 occupies the space between a full-fledged tablet and a low-distraction E-Ink device like the Remarkable Pro. It has a full color LCD screen with a 120Hz refresh rate. You can watch videos and scroll a website as you normally would — something that just doesn’t work on E-Ink tablets. But the A1 is a note-taking device first and foremost, shipping with a pressure-sensitive stylus with adjustable haptics to mimic the scratchy feeling of writing on paper. It’s not like, “I can’t believe it’s not real paper” levels of convincing, but it’s good enough that you can lose yourself in the act of writing. I did, at least, enough to forget about the “eraser” on the other end of the stylus. Unfortunately, the Note A1 falls into the classic trap of trying to offer the best of both worlds: it ends up feeling like it’s not quite here nor there. As a tablet, it’s just okay. Its 8GB of RAM are enough to help it chew through a media-dense web page with a little juddering. The LCD is honestly nicer than I expected, with generous viewing angles and vivid colors. But its blacks aren’t as rich as an OLED’s, and a little dimming in one corner of my review unit gives it away. The built-in speakers are fine in a pinch but sound tinny, and there are no physical volume buttons, which is a bizarre thing to omit. [Image: The stylus attaches magnetically to the side of the tablet, where it also charges. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268711_TCL_Note_A1_Nxtpaper_review_AJohnson_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] As an e-reader and note-taking device, it does the job but lacks the precision of a purpose-built device like the Remarkable. The home screen looks like a generic notes app’s main screen, plus a collapsible side panel where you can access other apps and system settings. I love a minimalist home screen as much as the next overstimulated millennial, but I wish it was more customizable. You can hide the two widgets at the top of the screen, including the “Inspiration Space” (more on that later) and change how your assortment of note collections appear, but you can’t do much more than that. Neither can you create your own cover design for your note collections — you’re stuck with some bland options that have TCL branding on them. TCL’s Max Ink Mode also would have been a nice addition here. The company’s other Nxtpaper tablets and phones offer this monochrome mode to simulate more of an e-reader experience and extend battery life by a lot. I’m surprised it’s missing.   I also had trouble while writing out a note and kept accidentally triggering the “back” navigation gesture at the side of the screen while writing this review. (Spoiler alert: I wrote my whole first draft on the tablet itself. Please applaud.) TCL doesn’t offer a way to disable this while writing, and though the notes app always saved my work before exiting, it was jarring. Still, the A1 has some standout strengths. It comes with a massive 8,000mAh battery and will easily hold up to a couple of days of continuous use. There’s a toggle in quick settings to turn on an eye comfort mode to cut down on blue light, and you can adjust the color temperature warmth to your liking. The stylus’ pressure sensitivity feels restrained yet responsive. I had the best time with the A1 when I forgot all about its tablet-ness and just embraced it as a canvas for doodles and writings. The A1 has a suite of AI features that all sound pretty familiar by now. With a dedicated button on the stylus you can highlight text and images to add to the “Inspiration Space,” a repository for things you might otherwise keep in a thousand idle Chrome tabs. You can group these clippings, along with your notes and doodles, into collections. Reminiscent of Pixel Screenshots, it uses AI to analyze and tag the items you add so you can cross-reference them and find it all later. I gave it an honest try and used it to organize some information and #inspo for my endless yard project. I recorded audio of a call with our landscape designer, running the transcript on one side of the screen and hand-writing notes on the other. This is exactly the kind of scenario tech companies love to pitch for devices like this, and yeah, it was neat. The voice transcription was very good, and an AI-generated summary of the call caught all the main takeaways. I had a harder time getting useful analysis from the AI in the Inspiration Space. I put the call transcript and all my related doodles and screenshots into a folder, thinking I’d be able to tap the ever-present “Ask AI” chip for some high-level analysis. It failed to identify the images I’d added and played dumb when I asked it questions it could have found answers to in the transcript. Bummer. [Image: This keyboard case is unfortunately not sold in the US right now. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268711_TCL_Note_A1_Nxtpaper_review_AJohnson_0005.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Aside from my disappointment with AI features — not for the first or last time! — I had a good time with the Note A1. I wish it came with Max Ink Mode. It’s not your best choice for a tablet-first, note-taking-second device. There’s an iPad for that. And Remarkable offers a better writing and note-keeping experience for purists. But if you’re after a decent digital writing experience and still want tablet features on the side, the A1 does the job. Certainly for a lot less money than an iPad Air or Pro with an Apple Pencil Pro — that combo will start just under $900 and only goes up from there. I think the best endorsement I can give of the Note A1 is that I enjoyed it enough to write out my entire review on it by hand. I think it will also be the last blog I write out by hand, but it was pretty satisfying. You just don’t get the same effect with a Google Doc. Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

articles.title: The OLED Xbox Ally X20 officially starts at $1,300
articles.summary: You can pre-order a standalone Xbox Ally X20 handheld with OLED screen at Best Buy or Asus’s online store for $1,300, shipping October 15th.
articles.body: The Asus Xbox Ally X20 looked like it could be one of the best handheld gaming PCs yet made — but originally, Asus wanted you to buy a bundle pairing it with pricy AR glasses. In July, we told you that bundle would no longer be necessary, and today it’s official: you can pre-order a standalone handheld at Best Buy or Asus’s online store for $1,300, shipping October 15th. Asus spokesperson Don Nguyen tells us it’s the same basic ROG 20th Anniversary handheld I tried at its US offices, so you should be getting a translucent gadget with gold trim. Bling isn’t the reason to buy it, though. If I were buying, it’d be because of the larger new 7.4-inch 1080p OLED screen, the clearest, fastest, and brightest on a handheld yet. I’d be buying for the extra-comfy grips, the trick D-pad that rotates between 4-way and 8-way, and the lack of an Xbox “Library” button to yank me out of my game. You can read my full preview here, though I always recommend waiting for the reviews — my review of the rival MSI Claw EX found issues that were invisible in my preview, after all. Personally, I think $1,300 is an awful lot to spend on a handheld, but I’m pleased that it “only” costs $300 more than the original $1,000 Xbox Ally X, especially since that $1,000 model and the $600 Xbox Ally will continue to stick around, Asus rep Anthony Spence confirms. But if you have $2,500 to spend, Asus is making the bundled version a bit more attractive. Not only will it include the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 and a matching pair of 240Hz ROG XREAL X1 glasses (normally $849), it’ll also come with a matching Dbrand Killswitch protective case for the handheld (with the hardshell screen cover, stick toppers and built-in kickstand), plus a branded Pelican case to carry everything in. Here’s the bundle: [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/ROG-XBOX-Ally-X20-Bundle-Set.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] And here’s another photo of the Dbrand Killswitch around the handheld: [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Front-Kickstand-Deployed.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Xbox Ally X20 won’t be the most powerful handheld (that’ll currently be a Strix Halo device like the upcoming $1,750 GPD Win Max 3) or even the most powerful handheld that feels properly portable (that’ll be the Claw EX), and it certainly won’t be the most affordable. But it might be the most refined and comfortable to use among Windows handhelds. We’ll find out this fall.

articles.title: Asus' Special Gold ROG Xbox Ally X20 Is Surprisingly Affordable – If You Avoid the Bundle

And, while the company's special anniversary version of the Xbox Ally X is a bit more expensive than the regular version, it's not by much.
articles.body:
While everything seems to be going up in price lately due to an ongoing RAMageddon that doesn't seem to be letting up any time soon , Asus' handhelds have somehow avoided the price increases that are hitting everything in the category. The company's special anniversary version of the Xbox Ally X is a bit more expensive than the regular version, but it's not by much.

At gamescom , Asus revealed a bit more information about the upcoming gold-themed version of the Xbox Ally X to celebrate ROG's 20th anniversary, called, what else, the Xbox Ally X20. This is essentially the same system as the original Xbox Ally X , just with an OLED display, TMR joysticks, and a fancy new D-pad. Okay, well at least the innards remain the same, with the AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme and 24GB of memory.

Back when Asus announced the X20, I was worried this was going to be a sneaky way to refresh the handheld with a couple new features to raise the price to the same degree as something like the Lenovo Legion Go 2 or the Steam Deck — especially since, back then, it was announced as only part of a bundle with the Asus ROG Xreal R1 glasses I reviewed a few weeks ago.

Luckily, Asus will be releasing the Xbox Ally X20 as a standalone handheld for $1,299, or as a bundle with the glasses for $2,499. That is more expensive than the existing Xbox Ally X, which you can get for about $999 right now. But, that extra $300 might be worth it just for the sake of having an OLED display.

The new handheld looks like it'll take some cues from the Xbox Elite controllers as well. The Xbox Ally X20 will have a transforming D-pad. Basically, you can rotate it to choose between either a concave D-pad or one with four prounounced cardinal directions. Basically, like you're able to do on the Xbox Elite controllers by swapping out the magnetic D-pad.

Of course, the handheld is going to look much fancier than the original. I haven't seen it in person yet, but from Asus' photos, it looks like it has a translucent chassis, with gold accents that really do make it look unique.

The elephant in the room, though, is the bundle. It costs twice as much, and includes the glasses and a few accessories. Everything does look nice, but you're essentially paying an extra $1,200 for a pair of XR glasses that you can buy seperately for $849 – and those were already overpriced. It's going to carry some weight for ROG faithfuls, but the standalone handheld is where it's at. The Xbox Ally X is one of the best Windows handhelds out there, and tacking on an OLED display really might be worth the extra $300, especially with every other handheld with similar specs being closer to $2,000 right now.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: The First PlayStation Monitor Is Here and It's Great for PS5 Fans, but PC Players Won't Find Much to Love
articles.summary: Sony’s first PlayStation monitor has landed. It’s surprisingly modest and practically useful, but is it worth paying extra for?
articles.body:
The separation between PC and console gaming is hazier than ever thanks to soaring prices, scarce hardware, and PC ports of formerly exclusive games. Go into the average PC gamer’s home and you’re likely to find at least one console, and that’s exactly the crowd that Sony hopes to appease with its new PlayStation 27” gaming monitor. Designed to match the look of your PS5 or PS5 Pro perfectly, it packages a QHD resolution with high refresh rate gameplay, auto-HDR, and a foldaway charging dock for your DualSense controllers for $349.99. If you’re a PlayStation fan, it’ll make a great addition to a desk-based gaming setup. If you don’t care about its PS5 look, however, this really isn’t the monitor you’re looking for.

Sony PlayStation 27" Gaming Monitor – Hands-On Photos

It only takes a second to see who the monitor is aimed at. Between the black stand and white back of the monitor itself, it’s a perfect match for the PS5. The branding is minimal: a simple PS logo that peeks out above the stand when viewed from the rear.

The monitor comes perilously close to looking boring from the front. It’s the usual profile we’ve seen on flat panel gaming displays for years, with vanishingly thin bezels that lend the display a feeling of spaciousness. There are no visible controls. Toggling settings in the OSD is done with a joystick in the back. In short: black rectangle.

That is, until you start using the display’s biggest console-specific feature: its DualSense charging hook. Centered behind the display is a flip-down charging dock to store and charge your DualSense and DualSense Edge controllers when not in use. It sounds small — it is small — but it’s exactly the kind of quality-of-life feature that PS5 players will appreciate. No more loose controllers or wires to clutter up your desk, just your neatly glowing DualSense under your now very PlayStation-looking monitor.

As the first real PlayStation-branded monitor (Sony Inzone also offers PC gaming monitors but is a separate line from PlayStation), I expected Sony to go big: OLED, high refresh rate, high peak brightness, and an even higher price. Instead, it went the opposite direction by offering something entirely more accessible to the average person.

Coming in at $350, it offers some pretty decent specs no matter which platform you choose. Within its slim frame, it features an IPS panel with a sharp 2560x1440 resolution. It’s built for everything from turn-based RPGs to twitch shooters, sporting a quick 240Hz refresh rate on PC and 120Hz on console (the PlayStation 5’s peak output). It also comes with Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) support so your gameplay stays fluid. It’s technically AMD FreeSync, but worked well with Nvidia G-Sync too.

While it’s not OLED, its Fast IPS panel is a good example of why you should still be paying attention to this tech. The colors are vibrant and the viewing angles are wide. It features a 1ms gray-to-gray response time which won’t get you the exceptional motion clarity of OLED but is effective at keeping ghosting away. Sony also did a good job calibrating the display from the factory. Out of the box, I measured color accuracy to be just under the industry standard of Delta E < 2, so you could even use it for image or video editing.

Around the back, the monitor’s I/O is neatly tucked away. It comes with two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 1.4, and a couple of USB Type-A ports and one Type-C to support peripherals and accessories. The charging hook folds away just below this, so if you tend to keep your monitor low, you may need to raise it when the hook is in use.

The stand is disappointing for the price. It’s a flat metal slab and a vertical metal tube and that’s about it. You’re able to make the usual tilt and height adjustments and rotate it but you can’t pivot into a portrait orientation. It does support standard VESA 100x100 mounts, so finding a replacement isn’t difficult if it bothers you.

The monitor has a few other PlayStation-specific tricks up its sleeve, like Auto HDR Tone Mapping which automatically adjusts the console’s HDR settings to match on setup. Also, it has a built-in speaker so you can hear your games even if you don’t feel like plugging in a headset. That shouldn’t be novel, but it’s not a given anymore. Without the connection to PlayStation, it’s not a display that would have more than a headphone jack in most cases.

But you should still use a headset. While it’s admirable that Sony included a speaker here, it feels like a “break glass in case of emergency” kind of addition instead of something I would actually recommend you use. The sound is thin and tinny, and I found it harsh to listen to for very long. It will work in a pinch, but even a cheap gaming headset will perform leagues better.

Though the PlayStation 27" gaming monitor doesn't feel cheap necessarily, there is a sense that Sony pared things back to make it as affordable as it is. The cheap stand is one example, but it shows through in other ways too.

The OSD, for example, is basic and feels too generic for a monitor like this. It's functional, but it doesn't carry the same premium touch as the hardware around it. There are a couple of neat things you can do, like displaying your frame rate in the corner or automatically changing color profiles to match the genre of the game you're playing, but beyond that, it's standard fare: brightness, contrast, saturation, sharpness, inputs and outputs, volume, and so on. It gets the job done, but it won't wow anyone navigating through the menus. Unlike the Inzone monitors, there’s also no software to allow you to make adjustments with a mouse and keyboard.

Another is the same IPS panel I was praising earlier. While those pros are definitely there, there are some cons to be aware of too. There’s nothing special about this monitor’s contrast. It’s edge-lit, no full array local dimming, so blacks can be inconsistent across the display. No matter where you’re looking, black looks closer to dark gray and it earns its decidedly average 1000:1 contrast ratio.

Its average rated brightness, 350 nits, is decidedly middle of the road. It’s not bright enough to match the highlights and shadows of most TVs these days, but does find a balance between console and PC play. When you’re playing on your PS5, the auto HDR tone mapping allows the display to better represent highlights and shadows, offering more detail within the picture. On PC, there’s no automatic tone mapping but I did find that it was bright enough to use in a well lit room.

I was able to spend about a week with this monitor ahead of this review, and I hit it hard during that time. I set up the PS5 in one input and an RTX 5090 gaming laptop in another to see how it would handle switching between both platforms. Perhaps expectedly from a company well known for its displays, it performed well for both and a fair share of productivity in between.

While it might seem like a missed opportunity to go with QHD (1440p) resolution and not 4K, I think going QHD was the smart move. 1440p sits in a sweet spot where it looks crisp and detailed on 32” monitors or below but isn’t so demanding that you need the most expensive hardware to make the most of it. There aren’t many PCs capable of running many games at 240Hz without dramatically lowering settings — a major trade-off if you’ve already shelled out for a decent gaming PC and a new monitor. At QHD, that suddenly becomes much more attainable.

Playing on the PlayStation 5, I was impressed at how well the auto tone mapping feature worked. It's not HDR, but it’s better than SDR, and that alone is an improvement over the average gaming monitor at this price. My console had no trouble detecting the monitor and its capabilities, so enabling VRR and 120Hz only required a quick trip to the settings menu.

On PC, I felt the lack of quality HDR much more but gaming on it was still visually rich and a lot of fun. IPS colors are vivid and are perfectly capable of making games look great in SDR. VRR also worked well on both my Nvidia and AMD gaming laptops .

The charging hook also worked perfectly. It’s a simple system that allows you to quickly dock a controller without giving it much thought. Like other controller docks, it needs to work and get out of the way. This does that. Missed opportunity to give the hook a bit of accent lighting like the PS5 itself though, Sony.

Taken as a whole, the monitor delivers on its promises and does no more and no less. If you strip away all the PlayStation branding, what you’re left with is a decent monitor with a mediocre stand and cool charging hook. Plenty of monitors have USB ports and 1440p resolution. Plenty of monitors offer better brightness and better HDR with full array local dimming. Many of them cost under $350.

What the PlayStation monitor offers is a quiet guarantee that everything is going to work with a minimum of setup and fuss, especially with your PS5. It’s already going to blend in with part of your setup, and if you have your PS5 visible, you can count on them being a good looking pair.

The charging hook, as seemingly small and replaceable as it is, is probably the single most important feature for making it actually feel like a PlayStation monitor. Let’s be real here. You probably won’t be looking at the PS branded back of your monitor very often. Once you set it up with your PC, the auto tone mapping becomes something you don’t even think about shortly after. But the controller, pulsing with its little status light, is a constant reminder that you’re using a PlayStation accessory. And it’s useful to boot.

articles.title: GuliKit’s Switch 2 TV dock gives me one feature I’ve missed when traveling
articles.summary: GuliKit’s Switch 2 TV dock isn’t the smallest you can buy, but for $30, it gives me a safe place to perch my console while I’m gaming away from home.
articles.body: Nintendo didn’t design its Switch dock with travel in mind. Genki’s Covert Dock is a much smaller alternative my family has been using to connect our Switch to hotel TVs for years, but I’ve come to realize I much prefer having a stand for the console when using it this way. So when it came time to replace the Genki because Nintendo broke compatibility with the Switch 2, GuliKit’s updated travel dock seemed like a better fit for my needs. Like Nintendo’s, it provides a convenient place to perch the console while playing on a TV. It’s not perfect, but its few tradeoffs are easy to overlook given GuliKit’s solution is less than half the price of Genki’s. When I first unboxed the GuliKit Dock for Switch 2, it felt like a bait and switch. Although it looks like it’s milled from a block of aluminum like my MacBook, the dock is actually an all-plastic affair that’s convincingly finished to look like metal. Picking it up for the first time was akin to grabbing an empty soda can you think is full. It’s surprisingly light, and while I was initially disappointed, I soon realized that was probably a good thing since I’m an over-packer who frequently deals with overweight baggage. [Product: GuliKit Dock for Switch 2 | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GZNTFX7T?tag=theverge02-20] The dock’s design — essentially a square puck with rounded corners — is larger than the Genki dock I used to travel with, but it’s by no means bulky or cumbersome. It’s wide enough to securely support the Switch when it’s docked (I actually wouldn’t want it any smaller), and it positions the console at a slight backwards angle that helps ensure it won’t fall off and face-plant even if accidentally bumped. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] A magnetic cover protects the USB-C connector when it’s not in use, but while the Switch is connected, the cover can be attached to the top of the dock where it doubles as a slightly taller backrest for the console. It’s a good idea, but one let down by relatively weak magnets. It doesn’t take much force to dislodge the cover, and I’ve already had it pop off on its own while buried in my backpack. Attaching the cover with a hinge held shut by a single strong magnet would have worked better, I think. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] On the underside of the dock are four rubber feet preventing it from sliding around and a three-position sliding switch that’s supposed to extend the USB-C connector to accommodate your console when it’s in a protective case. On the dock I tested, moving that switch to different positions only served to slightly change the angle of the USB-C connector by a few degrees, which doesn’t seem all that useful. [Image: The dock includes HDMI, USB-C, and a USB-A port for charging accessories, plus a button that disables the video output so you can just use it as a charger. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] On the back of the dock is a 4K/60Hz HDMI port, a USB-A port for charging accessories like a controller, and a USB-C port for connecting an adapter with up to 100W of power delivery. Having to supply your own power adapter is the biggest downside to choosing GuliKit’s dock over Genki’s that has one built-in and is designed to plug straight into an outlet. That could make GuliKit’s dock less appealing to some, but it’s not an issue for me given I already travel with multiple adapters that deliver the 60W the Switch 2 needs for its dock mode. Alongside the multiple ports on the back is also a small button that turns off dock mode and video output so the accessory only functions as a charger. GuliKit positions this feature as a way to charge and play the Switch in handheld mode without actually having to hold it. While the ergonomics of that approach seem less than ideal to me, disabling the dock mode does have the benefit of making the Switch charge a little faster if you’re in a rush to top off its battery. [Image: The dock fits in the palm of your hand and is deceptively light, making it easy to travel with. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/gulikitdock2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] If you’re looking for the smallest possible way to connect your Switch 2 to a TV, you’re probably better off grabbing Genki’s or Jsaux’s accessories that incorporate a power adapter into their designs so all you need to provide is an HDMI and USB-C cable. GuliKit’s solution is slightly bulkier, but I really like that it replicates most of the functionality offered by the bundled Nintendo dock with a much smaller footprint. And it’s not just useful for traveling. If you want to connect your Switch 2 to TVs in multiple rooms around your home and don’t need an ethernet port, at $29.99 GuliKit’s is a much cheaper alternative to Nintendo’s $124.99 dock set, even when factoring in the added cost of an HDMI cable and 60W adapter. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: PlayStation Plus Monthly Games for September 2026 Leak, Headlined by Sniper Elite: Resistance
articles.summary: September's PlayStation Plus monthly games lineup has leaked online ahead of Sony's official announcement.
articles.body:
September's PlayStation Plus monthly games lineup has leaked online ahead of Sony's official announcement.

As detailed by Dealabs ' ever-reliable billbilk-kun, next month's list of titles available to PlayStation Plus subscribers will include last year's Sniper Elite: Resistance, placing you behind the long gun barrel of a British agent infiltrating Nazi-occupied Europe in 1944.

"A solid stealth-based shooter," is how IGN's Sniper Elite: Resistance review described the game, affording it a 6/10 score. "It fails to set its sights high enough in order to pull off a truly spectacular execution," we added.

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

Released back in 2022, the classic Japanese role-playing game inspired Chained Echoes is next on the roster. Inspired by classics such as Secret of Mana, Chrono Trigger and Final Fantasy 4, this retro-feeling RPG proudly wears its influences on its sleeve — but is no worse off for doing so.

Lastly, there's Wobbly Life. This colorful open-world sandbox launched last year and lets you muck about with friends to complete jobs, earn money, and own houses. All three games will be available from September 1 to October 6.

As a reminder, you still have until September 1 to claim August's trio of titles for PS Plus members. Those offerings include Dying Light 2 Stay Human: Reloaded Edition, Big Walk and Signalis.

articles.title: The Simpsons Parodies Black Mirror in New Disney+ Special
articles.summary: Ahead of the Season 38 premiere, The Simpsons is returning to Disney+ for a special episode that lampoons Black Mirror. Check out our exclusive preview of "Yellow Mirror."
articles.body:
The Simpsons will soon return for a mind-boggling 38th Season on Fox. But if you can't wait that long, you're in luck. The series is about to drop its latest exclusive episode on Disney+, and we've got an exclusive early look.

Check out the slideshow gallery below to see exclusive new images from "Yellow Mirror":

The Simpsons: "Yellow Mirror" Image Gallery

"Yellow Mirror" isn't the first Simpsons special to be exclusive to Disney+, but it is notable for being a full-length episode rather than a short in the vein of "The Simpsons in Plusaversary." As the title suggests, this episode acts as a spoof of Netflix's popular sci-fi anthology series Black Mirror. It features two tales linked by a common dystopian technology theme.

Here's the official description for "Yellow Mirror":

A defective lamp reveals a heartbreaking truth about what Homer believes is reality, and an AI-powered tablet befriends and controls Maggie. The Simpsons struggle to find the light through two dark tales of the curious and bizarre in this Disney+ exclusive.

"Yellow Mirror" will premiere on Disney+ on Wednesday, August 26.

In other The Simpsons news, Bart Simpson voice actress Nancy Cartwright believes the series will ultimately end with Season 40 . The show also recently returned to Fortnite, where fans could collect a Simpsons-style John Wick skin .

Fans were also recently given new hope about the long-awaited return of The Simpsons: Hit & Run , with Matt Groening saying, "I think the original game is coming back in some form."

articles.title: KFC Reveals the Oreo Chicken Burger, and We're Both Revolted and Intrigued
articles.summary: Has capitalism gone too far? KFC China has just revealed the Oreo Original Recipe Chicken Burger, and we can't help but be intrigued.
articles.body:
If you're a fan of strange and unholy fast food concoctions, then you'll definitely want to see what the crazed scienticians at KFC and Nabisco have concocted. Fresh off the reveal of their fried chicken-flavored Oreo cookies in China, the two companies have reversed that fusion to create the Oreo Original Recipe Chicken Burger.

This bizarre collab was revealed by KFC China on Weibo ( via Dexerto ). It looks every bit as strange as it sounds. The sandwich starts off ordinarily enough, with a fried chicken patty and lettuce, but it's topped with brown mashed potatoes dusted in cookie crumbles and placed between two Oreo cookie-flavored buns.

Like any good fast food mash-up, we can't decide if we're grossed out by this creation or deeply intrigued. Either way, American foodies shouldn't count on being able to try the Oreo Original Recipe Chicken Burger anytime soon. The sandwich is currently limited to the Chinese market only, with no indication of when or if it might come to the US.

Will you devour an Oreo Chicken Sandwich if given the opportunity? Cast your vote in our poll below:

This is just the latest odd creation from the folks at Nabisco. Past Oreo cookie variants have included Post Malone Oreos , which featured swirled salted caramel and shortbread flavored cream squeezed between one golden and one chocolate Oreo wafer cookie, and Mario Oreos . And in perhaps the most unholy combination of them all, there's the Ritz Oreo .
